blurb: Giving models fresh, citable knowledge: chunking, retrieval, reranking and where RAG goes wrong.

cards.title: Open-book answers

steps.p: A model only knows what was in its training data, frozen at a cutoff date, and it may misremember details.
RAG searches a document collection for passages relevant to the question and pastes them into the prompt.
The model answers using that text and can cite it, so users can check the claim.

cards.aside: It is the difference between a closed-book and an open-book exam.

cards.q: For answering questions about your company's documents, RAG's main advantage over fine-tuning is that…
options: Documents can be updated instantly and answers can cite sources, with no retraining
It is always cheaper per query
cards.why: Freshness and traceability. Change a document and the next answer reflects it. Fine-tuning bakes facts into weights, where they are hard to update or trace.

cards.statement: RAG updates the model's weights with the retrieved documents.
cards.why: False. Retrieved text is only added to the prompt. The model is unchanged; it reads the passages like any other input.

cards.title: The term "retrieval-augmented generation" comes from a 2020 Facebook AI paper.
cards.detail: Patrick Lewis and colleagues coined it. Lewis later said in an interview that they would have picked a nicer name had they known how widespread it would become.

cards.why: False — it reduces them. The model can still misread a passage, merge sources incorrectly, or ignore the context. And if retrieval returns the wrong passages, the answer is built on the wrong facts.

options: The date after which events are absent from its training data
When the company stops supporting it
cards.why: The edge of its training data. Anything after it is unknown unless supplied in the prompt, for example by search or RAG.

cards.title: Preparing documents for search

steps.p: Documents are cut into passages, often a few hundred tokens each, sometimes with overlap between neighbors.
Each chunk is turned into a vector and stored, along with metadata such as source, date and section.
Many systems also build a keyword index, so exact terms like product codes can be found.

cards.aside: Chunking choices quietly decide how good the whole system can be.

cards.q: What is the main problem with chunks that are too small?
options: They lose surrounding context, so a passage may not make sense alone
cards.why: Lost context. A sentence like "It rose 12% that year" is useless without knowing what "it" is. Too-large chunks have the opposite problem: diluted meaning and wasted prompt space.

cards.q: Why do many pipelines overlap neighboring chunks?
options: So ideas that span a boundary aren't cut in half
cards.why: Boundary protection. A small overlap means a sentence split across two chunks still appears whole in at least one of them.

cards.title: Adding a sentence of document context to each chunk before embedding greatly improved retrieval in Anthropic's tests.
cards.detail: Its 2024 "contextual retrieval" method had a model write a short note situating each chunk in its document. Combined with keyword search, it reported about 49% fewer failed retrievals, rising to 67% with reranking.

cards.statement: A vector database is required to build RAG.
cards.why: False. Any retrieval works: keyword search, SQL queries, a web search API, even grep over files. Vectors are common, not mandatory.

cards.q: The classic BM25 keyword ranking scores a document higher when it…
options: Contains the query's terms, especially rare ones, several times
cards.why: Term frequency weighted by rarity. Matching a rare word counts more than matching "the". BM25 also normalizes for document length and caps the gain from repeats.

cards.title: Retrieve wide, then rerank

steps.p: Embedding search quickly pulls the top 50 or 100 candidates from millions of chunks.
A reranker reads the query and each candidate together and scores how well it actually answers the question.
Only the top handful go into the prompt, saving context and reducing distraction.

cards.aside: Cheap and broad, then expensive and precise — a pattern used across all of search.

cards.q: Why are cross-encoder rerankers more accurate than embedding search?
options: They read the query and document together, so attention can compare them word by word
They are trained on more data
cards.why: Joint reading. Embedding search encodes query and document separately and compares two summaries. A cross-encoder sees both at once and can judge relevance precisely.

cards.statement: Rerankers are usually too slow to run over an entire document collection.
cards.why: True. They need a full model pass per query-document pair. That is fine for 50 candidates, impossible for 10 million — hence the two-stage design.

options: How often a relevant passage appears in the top 10 results
cards.why: Did we find it? If the right passage is not in what you retrieve, the generator cannot use it. Recall@k is the first number to check in a failing RAG system.

cards.statement: If a RAG system gives a wrong answer, the problem is usually the language model.
cards.why: Often false. Many failures are retrieval failures: the right passage never reached the prompt. Diagnose retrieval and generation separately.

cards.title: Check the citation, not just the answer
cards.body: A confident answer with a citation can still cite the wrong passage. Opening the source takes seconds and catches the most common RAG failure.
cards.challenge: Next time an AI tool cites a source, open it and confirm the cited text actually says what the answer claims.

cards.title: Smarter retrieval

steps.p: Instead of one fixed lookup, the model decides what to search, reads results, and searches again with better queries.
Vague or conversational questions are rewritten into search-friendly queries before retrieval.
Microsoft's GraphRAG (2024) extracts entities and relationships into a graph to answer questions about a whole collection.

cards.aside: The trend: retrieval is becoming something the model does, not something done to it.

cards.q: GraphRAG was designed for questions like…
options: "What is the phone number on page 4?"
"What are the main themes across all of these documents?"
cards.why: Global questions. Plain RAG retrieves a few passages and cannot summarize an entire corpus. Graph communities with pre-written summaries let the system answer big-picture questions.

cards.statement: Now that models have million-token context windows, RAG is obsolete.
cards.why: False. Most collections are far bigger than any window, and stuffing huge contexts is slow and costly. Retrieval also keeps answers fresh and citable.

cards.q: The HyDE technique improves retrieval by embedding…
options: A hypothetical answer the model writes, rather than the question itself
cards.why: A fake answer. Answers resemble other answers more than questions do, so a model-written draft lands closer to real answer passages in embedding space.

cards.title: A single planted document can hijack a RAG system.
cards.detail: Researchers (Greshake et al., 2023) showed that text with hidden instructions, once retrieved into the prompt, can steer an assistant's behavior — called indirect prompt injection.

cards.statement: A question and its correct answer always produce very similar embeddings.
cards.why: False. They are phrased differently and contain different information. That asymmetry is why retrieval models are trained on question-passage pairs and why tricks like HyDE help.
